title: Filtering With BETWEEN
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of filtering with between.
Apply inclusive range comparisons in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn filtering with between through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Filtering With BETWEEN matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of filtering with between is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Inclusive range comparisons, Numeric ranges, Date ranges, Range boundaries and timestamps. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Inclusive range comparisons
items.text: Inclusive range comparisons helps you express precise conditions with comparison, logical, range, membership, pattern, NULL-safe, and CASE expressions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Numeric ranges
items.text: Numeric ranges works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Date ranges
items.text: Date ranges needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Range boundaries and timestamps
items.text: Range boundaries and timestamps needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Choosing suitable interval boundaries
items.text: Choosing suitable interval boundaries helps you express precise conditions with comparison, logical, range, membership, pattern, NULL-safe, and CASE expressions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT employee_id, full_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000
ORDER BY salary;
content_blocks.expected_output: BETWEEN includes both endpoints. Use timestamp half-open intervals when inclusive upper bounds could miss fractional seconds.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
